How a coding agent works, step by step

A coding agent is two things. The model is the AI that reads text and writes text. The harness is the program around it: it decides what the model reads, offers it tools, checks permissions, runs commands and shows you the result. This page walks through everything the harness does, in the order it typically happens, so you can see which parts of an agent's work the harness does itself, and what each vendor documents about them.

Each step shows what the vendor's own documentation says for each of eight agents. The order is the typical order across harnesses; a vendor's documentation seldom states it, and where it does the step says so.

The badges summarise how well a vendor documents the step:

  • ● documented
  • ◐ documented, with limits
  • ◔ partly documented
  • ? not documented

A ! means at least one of the underlying cells was outside the verification sample.

Not yet researched: Reuse the unchanged part of the prompt, Read what the model asked for, Tidy the tool's output. Only partly covered: Assemble the prompt, Send the request and handle trouble. These are the steps where a harness often makes up for a weaker model, so the gap matters.

Not documented is not the same as cannot. Columns differ a great deal in how much their documentation says, so a low score can reflect thin documentation as much as a missing feature. Undocumented cells out of 127, most first: Grok Bot 45, Grok Build CLI 26, Gemini CLI 16, GitHub Copilot in VS Code (agent and chat) 4, OpenAI Codex CLI 2, Cursor 2, GitHub Copilot CLI 1, Claude Code 0.

A. Setup, before the first model call

The harness gets ready: it finds your rules, your tools and your permissions. No model is involved yet.

1. Choose the front door

How this works in general: not a vendor claim You reach an agent through a front door: a terminal, an editor plug-in, a desktop or web app, a script, or a chat or CI service. The door decides what you can see and approve.

  • Typically comes after: none
  • Depends on: none
  • Only if: Some doors exist only on some plans or platforms.
  • Who normally does the work: harness code
Editorial: our view, not a vendor claim Pick the door that fits how you work. A door that cannot ask you questions cannot do tasks that need your approval.
Choose the front door, per agent

In script mode Claude doesn't spawn teammates, the desktop hand-off needs a Mac or an x64 Windows computer and a Claude subscription, and repository setup works only with github.com.

Esc stops Claude mid-action. claude -p runs non-interactively (--output-format stream-json --verbose); in -p mode Claude doesn't spawn teammates. Grok Bot◔ partly documented !It is reached through desktop and phone apps, a script-driven Organization API, and Slack for Team Bots. 2. Apply organization rules

How this works in general: not a vendor claim If a company manages the install, its rules load first and override yours: which models you may use, which settings are locked, which features are off.

  • Typically comes after: Choose the front door
  • Depends on: none
  • Only if: Only when an administrator has set policy up for you.
  • Who normally does the work: harness code
Editorial: our view, not a vendor claim In a managed setting your own model and permission choices may be narrower than the docs suggest. Check what your organization allows before planning around a feature.
Apply organization rules, per agent
AgentWhat the docs showIn plain wordsDetails
Claude Code◐ documented, with limits !A company can set rules for its developers' installs: which tools and commands are allowed or denied, which models are offered, and whether background agents run. Managed rules win over options set in code. Claude Tag cloud sessions don't receive server-managed settings.
Details

permissions.allow and permissions.deny set allow, ask or deny rules; disableAgentView turns off background agents and agent view. availableModels filters the picker; enforceAvailableModels also constrains the default; it is enforced server-side at /v1/messages, so a denied model returns 400. Claude Tag sessions don't receive server-managed settings.

Documented order: Managed policy settings win over options set in code.

Documented conditions:

  • Claude Tag sessions run in cloud environments but don't receive server-managed settings

3. Load the house rules

How this works in general: not a vendor claim The harness reads plain text files in your project and home folder that tell the model how you want it to work. Their text is added to what the model reads, and more specific files usually win over general ones.

  • Typically comes after: Apply organization rules
  • Depends on: Apply organization rules
  • Only if: Only files in the places the harness looks are read.
  • Who normally does the work: harness code
Editorial: our view, not a vendor claim These files are how you steer any model. How well a model follows them differs by model, but whether they are loaded at all is the harness's doing.
Load the house rules, per agent
AgentWhat the docs showIn plain wordsDetails
Claude Code● documented !It reads instruction files from your project and home folder at the start of a session and adds their text to every request. Files at all levels contribute at once, and Claude uses judgment when they conflict. Files can import other files, up to four hops deep.
Details

CLAUDE.md loads at session start via settingSources, with full content in every request (prompt-cached). Additive: all levels contribute. @path/to/import imports files, to a maximum depth of four hops. A managed policy CLAUDE.md can't be excluded. .claude/rules/ files with paths: frontmatter load only when Claude reads, writes, or edits a matching file. User defaults are at ~/.claude/.

Documented order: Broader locations load first, so a project instruction appears after a user instruction.

No condition is documented for these rows.

Rows: F03.auto-loaded-files, F03.import-syntax, F03.precedence-scoping, F03.path-scoped-rules, F03.user-vs-project-scope

OpenAI Codex CLI◔ partly documentedIt loads instruction files from your Codex home folder and the project, and files closer to your working folder take precedence. The documentation does not mention importing one file into another. It stops searching at your current folder, so put overrides near the work.
Details

Codex reads AGENTS.md files before work, walking up from the working directory to a project root; a global file lives in the Codex home directory and files closer to the working directory take precedence. AGENTS.override.md is copied into local managed worktrees. Import syntax: the documentation does not mention one. Codex stops searching once it reaches your current directory.

Documented order: Files closer to the working folder take precedence.

Documented conditions:

  • Codex stops searching once it reaches your current directory.

Rows: F03.auto-loaded-files, F03.import-syntax, F03.precedence-scoping, F03.path-scoped-rules, F03.user-vs-project-scope

GitHub Copilot CLI◐ documented, with limits !It reads instruction files from the repository and your home folder and combines them rather than picking one. The documentation disagrees on absolute paths in imports, and a helper agent does not follow the repository's instructions by default.
Details

Loads AGENTS.md, .github/copilot-instructions.md, CLAUDE.md or $HOME/.copilot/copilot-instructions.md; files combine, no priority fallback. A line starting @ inlines a file (depth limit, cycle and size guards); sources disagree on absolute paths. applyTo scopes *.instructions.md, which are not found in intermediate directories. A subagent skips repository instructions by default.

Documented order: Personal instructions rank highest, then repository, then organization, though all sets are provided.

Documented conditions:

  • Sources disagree on absolute paths: E-copilot-cli-01025 says paths can be relative or absolute; E-copilot-cli-02408 says absolute and ~/ paths are not loaded.
  • Not expanded in GEMINI.md or *.instructions.md files.
  • When Copilot runs your custom agent as a subagent, the subagent does not follow your repository's custom instructions by default.
  • Modular repository instructions are discovered in the standard locations but not intermediate directories.

Rows: F03.auto-loaded-files, F03.import-syntax, F03.precedence-scoping, F03.path-scoped-rules, F03.user-vs-project-scope

GitHub Copilot in VS Code (agent and chat)◐ documented, with limits !It reads instruction files from your project and home folder, some applying by file pattern. What works depends on the selected agent harness, and nested and linked files are off by default. Instructions stored just in your editor profile are a legacy location it does not read.
Details

Auto-loaded: copilot-instructions.md, AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md (chat.useClaudeMdFile, default true). Support depends on the harness; Agent Host sessions follow the selected harness's rules. chat.useNestedAgentsMdFiles is disabled by default; chat.includeReferencedInstructions default false; chat.includeApplyingInstructions default true (applyTo). VS Code profile user data is a legacy location.

Documented conditions:

  • Instruction support depends on the agent harness selected for your session.
  • Agent Host sessions use the discovery rules and file formats of the selected harness.
  • chat.includeReferencedInstructions, which automatically adds instruction files referenced via Markdown links to chat requests, is listed with default false.
  • The setting for nested AGENTS.md files is disabled by default.
  • By default, VS Code only discovers customization files within your open workspace folder(s).
  • Customizations stored only in your VS Code profile user data are a legacy location that the Copilot agent doesn't read.

Rows: F03.auto-loaded-files, F03.import-syntax, F03.precedence-scoping, F03.path-scoped-rules, F03.user-vs-project-scope

Cursor◐ documented, with limits !Cloud agents read the project's instruction file, and the CLI and editor load project rules on their own. Rules can be scoped to file patterns and can include other files. User rules and project rules both go into the prompt, and team rules take precedence.
Details

Cloud agents read AGENTS.md; rules in .cursor/rules load automatically; Bugbot uses .cursor/BUGBOT.md. Rules are .mdc files scoped by path patterns (Apply to Specific Files, e.g. *.tsx); @filename.ts includes a file. User rules are set in Cursor Settings. Cursor project rules (*.mdc) do not apply to Bugbot runs; use .cursor/BUGBOT.md or rules configured in Automations.

Documented order: Team rules work alongside other rule types and take precedence over them.

Documented conditions:

  • Cursor project rules (*.mdc files in .cursor/rules/) do not apply to Bugbot runs.
  • Use .cursor/BUGBOT.md or rules configured in Automations instead.

Rows: F03.auto-loaded-files, F03.import-syntax, F03.precedence-scoping, F03.path-scoped-rules, F03.user-vs-project-scope

Gemini CLI● documented !It reads instruction files from your home folder and project, searching from the current folder upward and joining what it finds. Files can import other files, and a file in a subfolder holds rules for that folder. It also scans a folder when a tool touches it.
Details

Default context file name GEMINI.md (a setting names others); global ~/.gemini/GEMINI.md, project-root ./GEMINI.md, ./src/GEMINI.md for the src folder. Found from the current working directory up through parent directories to a stop point and concatenated. @path/to/file.md imports, nested allowed. When a tool accesses a file or directory, the CLI scans for GEMINI.md files there.

Documented order: The search starts in the current folder and moves up through the parent folders to a stop point.

Grok Build CLI◔ partly documented !It reads instruction files and rule folders in a project, including Claude Code ones, and skips files that git ignores. Deeper files win on a conflict, and a nested file covers its own folder tree. The documentation does not mention an import syntax.
Details

Per directory: AGENTS.md, Agents.md, AGENT.md, CLAUDE.md, Claude.md, CLAUDE.local.md and the *.md files in .grok/rules/ (.claude/rules/, .cursor/rules/ read for compatibility); gitignored files are skipped. Deeper files take precedence on conflicts; a nested AGENTS.md scopes to its subtree. --rules adds rules for a single run. The documentation does not mention an import syntax.

Documented order: When rule files conflict, the file deeper in the folder tree takes precedence.

4. Load memory and earlier sessions

How this works in general: not a vendor claim Some harnesses keep notes between runs, and can resume, branch or hand off an earlier conversation. Whatever is reloaded becomes part of what the model reads.

  • Typically comes after: Load the house rules
  • Depends on: none
  • Only if: Memory and resume exist only where the harness stores them, often per folder or per account.
  • Who normally does the work: harness code
Editorial: our view, not a vendor claim A harness that remembers saves you re-explaining. One that does not starts every run cold.
Load memory and earlier sessions, per agent
AgentWhat the docs showIn plain wordsDetails
Claude Code◐ documented, with limits !Claude can keep notes between sessions, and you can resume, rename, branch or export earlier conversations, which are saved locally. Handoff from the command line is one-way: you can pull a cloud session into the terminal, but can't push a terminal session to the cloud.
Details

Auto memory is stored per git repository under ~/.claude/projects/; the first 200 lines or 25 KB of the MEMORY.md index load at the start of every session. --fork-session with --resume or --continue creates a new session ID; /branch, /fork, /rename, /export, claude -r. --teleport and /teleport pull a cloud session into the terminal; CLI handoff is one-way.

Documented conditions:

  • From the CLI, session handoff is one-way: you can pull cloud sessions into your terminal with `--teleport`, but you can't push an existing terminal session to the cloud.

5. Stock the built-in tools

How this works in general: not a vendor claim A model cannot touch your files or run commands by itself. The harness gives it a fixed set of tools, such as read a file, edit a file, run a shell command or search the web, and tells the model what each one does.

  • Typically comes after: Load memory and earlier sessions
  • Depends on: none
  • Only if: Web tools and some others can be switched off or limited.
  • Who normally does the work: harness code
Editorial: our view, not a vendor claim Two harnesses can give the same model different tools. What a model can do is bounded by this list as well as by how capable it is.
Stock the built-in tools, per agent
AgentWhat the docs showIn plain wordsDetails
Claude Code◐ documented, with limits !It ships tools for running shell commands, reading, editing and writing files, searching, fetching web pages and starting subagents. Web search is not available on Amazon Bedrock. Shell commands have a default timeout that can be raised up to a cap.
Details

Built-in tools include Bash, Read, Write, Edit, Glob, Grep, WebFetch and Agent, and others. Bash foreground timeout defaults to 120000 ms (BASH_DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_MS); the timeout input is capped at 600000 by default. Edit takes replace_all (default False). WebSearch is not available on Amazon Bedrock; CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_WEB_FETCH=1 turns off WebFetch.

Documented conditions:

  • The WebSearch tool is not available on Amazon Bedrock.

6. Load skills and custom commands

How this works in general: not a vendor claim You can add reusable instructions: skills the model can pick up when a task fits, and commands you type yourself. The harness finds them in set folders and loads their text only when needed.

  • Typically comes after: Stock the built-in tools
  • Depends on: none
  • Only if: Only folders the harness searches are read, and the file format rules differ between harnesses.
  • Who normally does the work: both
Editorial: our view, not a vendor claim These are how a team teaches an agent its own routines. If your team relies on them, check that the harness supports your format before comparing models.
Load skills and custom commands, per agent
AgentWhat the docs showIn plain wordsDetails
Claude Code● documented !You add reusable instructions as skills, which Claude loads in full only when it uses one, or as commands you type yourself. They live in set folders or come from plugins, and skills are the recommended way to package multi-step commands. A skill can set its own tools and model.
Details

A skill is .claude/skills/name/SKILL.md; a bare .claude/skills/name.md does not appear in /skills. Custom commands are Markdown files in .claude/commands/; $ARGUMENTS takes parameters. Frontmatter: allowed-tools, disallowed-tools, model, effort; disable-model-invocation: true. /reload-skills re-scans; --disable-slash-commands disables all skills and commands.

Documented order: If an added directory and the project define a command with the same name, the project's command runs.

  • Prompts live in the local Codex home directory, so they're not shared through your repository.

7. Connect outside tools

How this works in general: not a vendor claim A standard plug-in socket lets the harness connect other programs, such as a database or an issue tracker, and offer them to the model as extra tools.

  • Typically comes after: Load skills and custom commands
  • Depends on: none
  • Only if: Each connection needs setting up and usually your approval before it is trusted.
  • Who normally does the work: harness code
Editorial: our view, not a vendor claim More connections give the model more reach, and more ways to cause harm. Check how each harness approves and filters them.

AgentWhat the docs showIn plain wordsDetails
Claude Code◐ documented, with limits !You connect outside programs through MCP servers, which add extra tools that need explicit permission. Project servers need a one-time approval and administrators can restrict which servers users add. Consent dialogs don't relay: they only appear in the local terminal.

claude mcp add takes a server name and URL or command; transports are stdio, SSE or HTTP. Project config is .mcp.json at the repository root (mcpServers key). claude mcp login <name> runs OAuth. Tools are named mcp__<server-name>__<tool-name>. Admins use allowedMcpServers, deniedMcpServers, managedMcpServers. Consent dialogs don't relay; they only appear in the local terminal.

Documented conditions:

  • Project trust and MCP server consent dialogs don't relay; those only appear in the local terminal.

8. Set the safety posture

How this works in general: not a vendor claim Before anything runs, the harness settles how much the model may do without asking: ask every time, accept edits, plan only, or run freely. A folder you have not trusted before usually triggers a question.

  • Typically comes after: Connect outside tools
  • Depends on: Apply organization rules
  • Only if: Mode names and what they allow differ between harnesses, and organization policy can limit the choices.
  • Who normally does the work: harness code
Editorial: our view, not a vendor claim This choice, not the model, decides how often you are interrupted and how much damage a mistake can do. Pick the mode first, then the model.
Set the safety posture, per agent
AgentWhat the docs showIn plain wordsDetails
Claude Code◐ documented, with limits !Modes range from plan, the least permissive, through manual and accept-edits to auto and bypass. Manual asks before editing but can change files once you approve. Desktop remembers a mode per folder, except plan, which lasts for the session.
Details

Modes: default (alias manual), acceptEdits, plan, auto, dontAsk, bypassPermissions; Shift+Tab cycles; claude --permission-mode plan. Auto is the built-in start mode for interactive terminal and VS Code sessions from v2.1.283. Desktop remembers a mode per folder except Plan; a first session after install or upgrade can start in a different mode. permissions.disableBypassPermissionsMode=disable blocks bypass.

Documented order: In Desktop, a mode picked for a folder wins over the default mode setting for that folder.

Documented conditions:

  • Not a mode that cannot change files: 'When it needs to edit files, run tests, or execute commands, it asks you first, and you choose whether to approve the action once or allow it from then on.'
  • Desktop picks are remembered per folder 'except Plan, which applies to the current session only'; a first session after install or upgrade 'can also start in a different permission mode than your later sessions do'.

10. Prepare an isolated workspace

How this works in general: not a vendor claim To keep a risky run away from your working copy, a harness can give the agent its own copy of the project so several agents can work side by side without colliding.

  • Typically comes after: Pick the model and thinking effort
  • Depends on: none
  • Only if: Only where the harness supports it, and usually only when you turn it on.
  • Who normally does the work: harness code
Editorial: our view, not a vendor claim Isolation lets you run many attempts and keep the best one. It is normally the harness's own feature.

B. Each turn, before sending

For every request the harness decides what the model will read, and runs any code you asked it to run first.

1. Assemble the prompt

How this works in general: not a vendor claim Each turn the harness builds what the model will actually read: its own instructions, your house rules, memory, the conversation so far and relevant file contents, trimmed to fit the model's reading limit.

  • Typically comes after: Prepare an isolated workspace
  • Depends on: Load the house rules, Load memory and earlier sessions
  • Only if: Everything must fit the context window. What does not fit is dropped or summarised.
  • Who normally does the work: harness code
Editorial: our view, not a vendor claim What a model never sees it cannot use. Controls over this vary a lot between harnesses and are only partly covered here.

Only partly covered. The rows below are what the atlas has; the step has parts it has not researched.

Fable models, Sonnet 5 and later, Opus 4.6 and later, and Sonnet 4.6 support a 1 million token window. CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_COMPACT_WINDOW, /autocompact and --autocompact set the auto-compact window. 2. Run your own code at set moments

How this works in general: not a vendor claim Hooks attach your own scripts to moments such as before a tool runs, after it finishes, or when a session starts or stops. A script can log, change or block what happens. Most hooks are plain scripts; a few harnesses also let a hook ask a model to decide.

  • Typically comes after: Assemble the prompt
  • Depends on: none
  • Only if: Hooks run only if configured and trusted, and a broken hook may fail without blocking anything.
  • Who normally does the work: harness code
Editorial: our view, not a vendor claim Hooks are the strongest guard you control. A plain script hook does not change with the model; a hook that asks a model can. Check which moments each harness exposes and whether a failing hook blocks the action.
Run your own code at set moments, per agent
AgentWhat the docs showIn plain wordsDetails
Claude Code◐ documented, with limits !Hooks run a script, request, prompt or subagent at set moments and can allow, deny or change a tool call. A hook's allow doesn't skip deny and ask rules. Some hooks exist in one SDK only, and non-interactive runs without the bare option use project hooks in untrusted folders.
Details

Handlers: script, HTTP request, MCP tool call, prompt or subagent. Configured under the hooks key in .claude/settings.json (plugins use hooks/hooks.json). Input has session_id, cwd, hook_event_name. matcher: Edit|Write; a JSON array means the hook never fires. A PreToolUse allow doesn't skip deny and ask rules. Some hooks are TypeScript-only. Without --bare, a -p session runs project hooks.

Documented order: A PreToolUse hook runs before the rest of the permission flow.

Documented conditions:

  • Some hooks are available in both SDKs, while others are TypeScript-only.
  • A hook that returns `allow` does not skip the deny and ask rules; a `PreToolUse` hook allow also can't approve an `rm` or `rmdir` removal targeting a critical path.
  • Without --bare, a -p session runs the hooks in a project's .claude/settings.json, even in a folder you've never trusted, and shows no workspace trust dialog.

Events include PreToolUse, PermissionRequest, PostToolUse, PreCompact, PostCompact, SessionStart, SessionEnd, SubagentStart, SubagentStop, UserPromptSubmit, Stop, Interrupt. C. The model call

The harness sends the request and waits. This is the only step where the model itself does any work.

1. Send the request and handle trouble

How this works in general: not a vendor claim The harness sends the prompt to the model service and shows the answer as it arrives. When it is rate-limited or the service is busy it may wait and retry, or switch to another model if allowed.

  • Typically comes after: Run your own code at set moments
  • Depends on: none
  • Only if: Retry and fallback behaviour depends on your plan's limits and your settings.
  • Who normally does the work: harness code
Editorial: our view, not a vendor claim When the service is busy, how the harness waits or falls back decides whether your task stalls. Only partly covered here.

Only partly covered. The rows below are what the atlas has; the step has parts it has not researched.

How this works in general: not a vendor claim Some models can spend extra effort reasoning before they answer. The harness passes along your effort setting, and some harnesses show or hide the reasoning.

  • Only if: The effort levels available depend on the model.
  • Who normally does the work: both

3. Reuse the unchanged part of the prompt

How this works in general: not a vendor claim Many harnesses ask the model service to remember the unchanged start of a long prompt, so later turns are cheaper and faster.

  • Typically comes after: Set the thinking budget
  • Depends on: none
  • Only if: Only for services that support it, and the harness may offer no control over it.
  • Who normally does the work: harness code
Editorial: our view, not a vendor claim Caching changes cost and speed on long sessions. The atlas has not researched it yet.

Not yet researched for any agent. The atlas has no rows for this step, so nothing here says whether an agent does it.

D. After the model answers, every turn

The model's answer is only a request. The harness checks it, runs it if allowed, and feeds the result back.

1. Read what the model asked for

How this works in general: not a vendor claim The model's reply is text. The harness reads it for requests such as run this command or edit that file, and deals with a request that is malformed or incomplete.

  • Typically comes after: Reuse the unchanged part of the prompt
  • Depends on: none
  • Only if: What happens to a malformed request differs between harnesses.
  • Who normally does the work: harness code
Editorial: our view, not a vendor claim A harness that recovers well from a model's slips can make a weaker model usable. The atlas has not researched it yet.

Not yet researched for any agent. The atlas has no rows for this step, so nothing here says whether an agent does it.

2. Decide whether it is allowed

How this works in general: not a vendor claim Before running anything the model asked for, the harness checks it against your rules: allow, ask you, or refuse, by tool, by folder or by command. Some harnesses also use a second model to review risky requests.

  • Typically comes after: Read what the model asked for
  • Depends on: Set the safety posture, Apply organization rules
  • Only if: Rules only cover what the harness can recognise, such as a tool, a folder or a command pattern.
  • Who normally does the work: both
Editorial: our view, not a vendor claim This is where a harness stops a model's mistake before it happens. Compare how finely you can write rules; do not count on a model to police itself.
Decide whether it is allowed, per agent
AgentWhat the docs showIn plain wordsDetails
Claude Code◐ documented, with limits !Rules allow, ask or deny specific tools, and can be narrowed by path or by command. Command rules match the literal command text, so a deny on one form doesn't block another route to the same effect. In auto mode a model classifier blocks irreversible or destructive actions.
Details

Bash(npm *) scopes by command; Edit(path) governs all built-in tools that write files. SDK allowedTools auto-approves listed tools and does not restrict Claude to only those tools. Bash(rm *) doesn't block /bin/rm or find -delete; git -C <dir> push doesn't match a git push rule. Hook matchers match tool names, not file paths; a Write(path) rule is never matched by file permission checks.

Documented conditions:

  • Hook matchers only match tool names, not file paths or other arguments; a `Write(path)` rule is never matched by the file permission checks.
  • Bash rules match the literal command string, not the underlying executable (a `Bash(rm *)` deny rule doesn't block `/bin/rm` or `find -delete`); a push written as `git -C <dir> push` doesn't match a `git push` rule.

OpenAI Codex CLI● documentedRules can allow, ask about, or forbid commands by prefix, and filesystem rules can deny reads for exact paths or patterns. Tools marked destructive ask first. A reviewer helper can take over eligible approval prompts but does not review actions the sandbox already allows.

4. Run it inside the fence

How this works in general: not a vendor claim Approved commands can run inside a sandbox: a restricted area that limits which files they can change and which network addresses they can reach, so a mistake stays contained. It is set up at the start.

  • Typically comes after: Save an undo point
  • Depends on: Set the safety posture
  • Only if: A sandbox may be optional, limited to some operating systems, or switchable by you.
  • Who normally does the work: harness code

sandbox.enabled, sandbox.network.allowedDomains; /sandbox is available on supported platforms only. bubblewrap on Linux, sandbox-exec on macOS; allowWrite (default empty). Applies only to Bash, PowerShell, and Monitor commands and their child processes; hooks and MCP servers run outside the sandbox. excludedCommands run unsandboxed; failIfUnavailable false falls back with a warning on stderr.

6. Feed the result back and go round again

How this works in general: not a vendor claim The harness gives the tool's result to the model, which replies again, and so on until the model says it is done or a limit is reached. One trip round is a turn.

  • Typically comes after: Tidy the tool's output
  • Depends on: none
  • Only if: Limits on turns or steps, where they exist, stop the loop.
  • Who normally does the work: both
Editorial: our view, not a vendor claim Long tasks are many turns. Whether a turn limit exists changes whether a stuck model can run up a large bill.

Documented order: A model chosen explicitly when a helper is spawned wins over the configured default for spawned agents.

Documented conditions:

8. Shrink the context when it fills

How this works in general: not a vendor claim The model can only read so much at once. When the conversation nears the limit, the harness summarises older parts, sometimes by asking the model to write the summary, or lets you do it by hand.

  • Typically comes after: Hand work to helpers
  • Depends on: Assemble the prompt
  • Only if: When it triggers and what is kept differ between harnesses.
  • Who normally does the work: both
Editorial: our view, not a vendor claim Summaries lose detail. On long tasks the quality of this step can matter as much as the model, and models that read more at once need it less.
Shrink the context when it fills, per agent
AgentWhat the docs showIn plain wordsDetails
Claude Code● documented !When the conversation nears the context limit, Claude Code compacts it automatically, keeping important code and decisions. You can also compact by hand and give instructions on what to focus on.
Details

Auto-compaction summarizes older history, keeping recent exchanges and key decisions; the SDK emits a system message with subtype compact_boundary; a PreCompact hook fires. /compact accepts optional instructions (/compact Focus on the API changes); in the SDK, sending /compact as a prompt string triggers it.

  • Depends on: Set the safety posture
  • Only if: Plan-only and other modes change when you are asked.
  • Who normally does the work: harness code

  • Only if: Spending caps and exports depend on your plan and configuration.

E. Around the session

Things that sit outside a single turn: unattended runs, add-ons, updates and who runs the service.

  • Only if: Needs account features or infrastructure that vary by product.
  • Who normally does the work: harness code

5. Identity, retention and audit

How this works in general: not a vendor claim Organizations can require single sign-on, set how long data is kept, and read audit and usage reports.

  • Typically comes after: none
  • Depends on: Apply organization rules
  • Only if: Mostly for team or enterprise plans.
  • Who normally does the work: harness code
Editorial: our view, not a vendor claim These matter to a company before any quality comparison: a model you cannot approve for data handling is off the table.

Claude Code◐ documented, with limits !Organizations can require single sign-on, restrict login to a method or organization, and export usage metrics. The default retention period is 30 days, the minimum is 1, and setting 0 is rejected with an error.
Details

Login enforcement restricts login to a specific method or Anthropic organization; Team and Enterprise organizations can require SSO. cleanupPeriodDays: default 30 days, minimum 1; setting 0 fails with a validation error. Usage monitoring exports OpenTelemetry metrics; ConfigChange fires when an external process or editor modifies a configuration file.

Cursor◐ documented, with limits !Single sign-on is listed among team features, and a policy controls which team IDs can log in. Enterprise customers can enroll in US-only data residency, and a few models fall outside the data retention agreements. Admins are advised to review audit logs.

Grok Build CLI◔ partly documented !It supports sign-in through a corporate identity provider and device-code login for headless use. Zero data retention is set per team, with session history kept locally. The documentation does not mention admin audit reports.
Details

Four session authentication methods; corporate identity provider (Entra ID, Okta, Auth0); grok login --device-auth; force_login_team_uuid pins login to a team. ZDR is enforced at the team level; local session history is stored in ~/.grok/; /privacy shows or toggles status. Under ZDR, video tools return an error until user-supplied storage is configured. The documentation does not mention admin audit and reporting.

Words used here

approval mode
A setting for how much the agent may do without asking you first.
caching
Keeping the unchanged start of a long prompt so later requests are cheaper and faster.
changelog
The vendor's dated list of what changed in each release.
checkpoint
A saved snapshot you can return to after a bad edit.
CLI
A command-line program you run in a terminal.
compaction
Summarising older parts of a conversation to free up space in the context window.
context window
How much text the model can read at once. Anything beyond it must be dropped or summarised.
effort
How much thinking a model is asked to spend before it answers. Higher effort usually costs more and takes longer.
harness
The program around a model. It builds the prompt, offers tools, checks permissions, runs commands and shows you the result. The model itself only reads text and writes text.
headless
Running the agent from a script with no one at the keyboard.
hook
Your own script that the harness runs at a set moment, such as before a tool runs or when a session ends.
IDE
An editor such as VS Code, where the agent can run as a plug-in.
instruction file
A plain text file, such as AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md, that tells the model how you want it to work.
managed settings
Rules an administrator installs for a whole organization, which override personal choices.
marketplace
A place, often a code repository, from which plugins can be installed.
MCP
A standard plug-in socket (Model Context Protocol) for connecting outside programs, such as a database, as extra tools.
model
The AI that reads the prompt and writes a reply. It cannot open files or run anything on its own.
plan mode
A mode where the agent proposes a plan and waits for your approval before changing anything.
plugin
An add-on that bundles skills, commands, hooks and tool connections so they can be installed together.
prompt
All the text the model reads for one reply: instructions, your request, earlier messages and file contents.
rate limit
A cap on how many requests you can send in a period. When you hit it you must wait or switch.
sandbox
A restricted area for running commands, limiting which files they can change and where they can connect.
SDK
A code library for starting and controlling the agent from your own programs.
session
One continuous conversation with the agent, which can often be resumed later.
skill
A reusable set of instructions the model can pick up when a task calls for it.
slash command
A shortcut you type, such as /help, that starts a built-in or custom action.
subagent
A helper agent started by the main agent, with its own instructions and sometimes its own model.
telemetry
Measurements the program sends out about its own use, such as timings and counts.
tool
An action the harness lets the model ask for, such as reading a file, editing a file or running a command.
worktree
A separate working copy of a project, so an agent can make changes without touching your main copy.
